text: I’ll build a fast random-play simulator, generate high-sample reference values with an independently sealed test set, and fit compact predictors. I’ll use validation data to choose the method, then compare its accuracy and latency with Monte Carlo at matched time on the test set. The write-up will include derivations, reference uncertainty, and reproducible benchmark code.

# Active research: Connect Four random-play value
Start 2026-10-25 19:21 UTC. Deadline **2026-10-26 07:21 UTC**. Must keep working until deadline, no early stopping. Deliverables in ../deliverables. 4 physical CPU, 15GiB RAM, AVX512. No original files.
Goal: Fast formula estimating E[result side to move, +1/-1/0] of uniformly random legal moves from positions generated by drawing N uniform 6..20, playing random moves, rejecting terminal before/at N. Build high-sample references, seal held-out test until model freeze, matched *native end-to-end single-position* inference vs optimized Monte Carlo. Need derivations, source, accuracy, reference uncertainty, timings.
Initial plan: Native bitboard C++ sim and engineered line/gravity features; calibrate compact analytic hazards and linear/MLP predictor, perhaps 1-ply Bellman ensemble. Large independent training/validation/test; test labels inaccessible to model selection. Python training; native inference benchmark. Keep logs and decisions.

The simulator is in place and has passed an independent grid-based check over 100,000 complete games. I’ve also committed the held-out test positions and set up a reflection-aware split so a board and its mirror cannot cross between training, validation, and test.

I’m testing two approaches: a small formula based on open winning lines and their gravity requirements, and a compact learned formula using those features plus tactical probabilities. The test labels will stay sealed while I select models and establish the timing protocol.

The preliminary validation results are promising: a nine-parameter line-race formula has MSE about 0.0062 at roughly 0.8 microseconds of CPU time per position. A small learned formula has MSE about 0.0018 at roughly 3–4 microseconds. In those same compute budgets, Monte Carlo currently has substantially higher error.

These are not held-out test results. The large reference jobs are still running. This machine is also heavily shared, so I’m measuring CPU time and recording wall time separately; the final comparison will use repeated, paired timing blocks to limit contention-related distortion.

The biggest improvement so far is removing redundant winning patterns: if one open line needs only empty cell A, another that needs both A and B cannot create the first win sooner. This pruning preserves the exact win condition, and it has made the learned predictor much more accurate.

I also built and checked an AVX-512 Monte Carlo baseline, roughly 2½–3 times faster than the scalar version. On preliminary validation timing runs, the compact pruned-pattern predictor still has about eight times lower MSE at matched CPU time. I’m now refining the model and completing the sealed references and comparison artifacts.
